Physician estimates of asthma severity may indeed be less accurate in Black patients compared to White patients. This disparity can contribute to racially disparate asthma care, where Black patients might receive underdiagnosed or undertreated asthma. Interventions to improve physicians' assessments and enhance patient-physician communication are crucial in minimizing racial disparities in asthma care.

The evidence suggests that paucigranulocytic asthmatics (those with a low eosinophil count) may be viewed as having low-grade inflammation, rather than being non-inflammatory. This nuanced understanding of the disease highlights the need for further research on the complexities of asthma phenotypes and the importance of considering patient-specific factors in clinical assessments.

Regarding higher body mass index (BMI), studies have shown that it does not necessarily contribute to worse asthma control in urban populations with asthma. Weight loss, however, may be a more effective strategy for improving asthma control in this group, as it has been demonstrated through validated questionnaires.
